extracted.intended_audience: researchers, scientometricians, journal editors, and policy makers interested in the reliability and evaluation of journal peer review
extracted.subtask_description: A multilevel meta-analysis synthesizing inter-rater reliability (IRR) estimates of journal peer review and identifying study-level determinants of variation in reported IRR. The paper evaluates measurement choices, study design features, and reporting practices that affect IRR estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-rater reliability (IRR) definition and target
rubrics_metrics.description: IRR is defined as “the extent to which two or more independent reviews of the same scientific document agree.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IRR is the central quality metric for peer review. The study reports low average IRR (.34 ICC/r; Cohen's Kappa = .17) and treats low IRR as a problem needing improvement (e.g., reader system). Interpret IRR in context — low values indicate substantial reviewer disagreement; high values may be suspect if based on small samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of reliability metric (ICC vs r vs Cohen's Kappa)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal quantitative IRR coefficients found in studies are Cohen's Kappa, intra-class correlation (ICC), and Pearson product-moment correlation (r); ICCs were preferred when available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICCs measure absolute agreement and consistency properly and are preferable when available. r can overestimate IRR unless reviewer means/variances are identical; to combine measures the square root of ICC or Fisher Z-transformed correlations can be used. Kappa has its own interpretation guidelines (Landis & Koch). Analysts must account for metric-specific properties when aggregating coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of Cohen's Kappa
rubrics_metrics.description: Cohen's Kappa indicates the proportion of agreement beyond chance; mean Kappa in the meta-analysis was .17.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow established interpretive guidelines (e.g., Landis & Koch) — a Kappa of .17 indicates 'slight' agreement. Use caution when comparing Kappa to ICC or r due to differing scales and properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample size / number of manuscripts as a determinant and bias test
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of manuscripts (sample size) used to compute IRR is an explicit covariate; larger sample sizes were associated with smaller reported IRR coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include sample size (often scaled, e.g., divided by 100) in analyses to detect publication bias: small studies tend to report higher IRR and are more likely to be published if results are large. Weight studies by inverse standard error; larger studies should have greater influence in meta-analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method-of-calculation covariate
rubrics_metrics.description: Method used to calculate IRR (ICC or r) was included as a covariate because different methods yield systematically different coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect method-driven differences; where necessary transform metrics (sqrt(ICC), Fisher Z) to achieve commensurability. Analysts should explicitly model the calculation method in meta-regression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline as a covariate
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific discipline (economics/law, natural sciences, medical sciences, social sciences) was included to test whether IRR varies by field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although some hypothesize higher IRR in 'hard' sciences, the meta-analysis found no significant discipline effect. Discipline should still be coded and tested (dummy-coded categorical variable) because theoretical expectations exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object of appraisal (abstracts vs papers) as covariate
rubrics_metrics.description: The object being appraised (e.g., abstracts submitted to conferences vs full papers submitted to journals) was included as a covariate because appraisal object may affect IRR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect different levels of agreement for different objects (abstracts may produce higher disagreement due to brevity), so code and test object type in analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohort / time period of data
rubrics_metrics.description: The period on which a study's data is based (cohort) was coded (e.g., decades) to test changes in IRR over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include cohort as a covariate to assess temporal trends in IRR; classify periods into meaningful categories to retain power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinding (single vs double) as a covariate
rubrics_metrics.description: Type of blinding (single-blind vs double-blind review) was tested for its effect on IRR; double-blind was hypothesized to increase agreement by removing bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although plausible, the meta-analysis found no significant effect of blinding on IRR (reviewers often identify authors). Still code blinding status for studies; consider masking success rates when interpreting null effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rating system characteristics and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Type of rating system (metric vs categorical, number of scale points) and whether the rating system information was reported were included as covariates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies that reported the rating system tended to show smaller IRR; failure to report rating system suggests lower study quality. Increasing the number of rating points may increase reliability. Always document rating instruments in primary studies; meta-analysts should code rating system detail (or 'unknown').

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting transparency / study quality indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Mentioning or not mentioning methodological basics (e.g., rating system) is treated as an indicator of study quality and relates to reported IRR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat detailed methodological reporting as a quality marker: lack of detail (e.g., no rating system description) is associated with inflated IRR and should be flagged as a potential quality problem in evidence synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical model choice for meta-analysis (fixed vs random vs multilevel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixed effects, random effects, and multilevel (three-level) models are described; multilevel models are recommended when studies report multiple dependent coefficients because they account for hierarchical dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multilevel models (e.g., manuscript/sample/study levels) to account for non-independence of multiple coefficients from the same study and to estimate within- and between-study variability. Random effects estimate the mean of a distribution of reliabilities; fixed effects assume a common true effect and are appropriate only when homogeneity is plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of meta-regression to explain heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: When between-study heterogeneity is high, include explanatory covariates in meta-regression (dummy-code categorical covariates; include an 'unknown' category for missing values to preserve power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run meta-regression models to identify covariates that explain heterogeneity (e.g., sample size, rating system). Follow recommendations on minimum number of studies per covariate to avoid overfitting. Compare models using log-likelihood and BIC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting studies by standard error in meta-analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies are weighted by the inverse of their standard error (so larger studies with smaller SE contribute more to the combined estimate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weighting reduces bias from small studies with large sampling error; empirically, this reduces the influence of small studies that tend to report higher IRR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of publication bias / file drawer problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication bias (tendency to publish studies with larger/more desirable results) is a key concern; sample size covariate was used to test for such bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test for publication bias and interpret high IRR from small-sample studies cautiously. Use sample size or funnel-plot-type approaches and include sample size as covariate in meta-regression to detect and adjust for bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number and selection of reviewers (including reader system)
rubrics_metrics.description: Increasing the number of reviewers to three or four, or using a 'reader system' of expert readers, was proposed and shown to increase IRR (e.g., single-rater reliabilities much higher in reader system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To improve reliability, use more reviewers or a structured reader system with selected experts. However, consider trade-offs: too much agreement may reflect redundancy, while diverse reviewer selection may lower IRR but improve validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off between reviewer agreement and validity (diversity of reviewers)
rubrics_metrics.description: High agreement is not always desirable; too much agreement can indicate redundant reviewers and reduced validity. Selecting reviewers for complementarity may lower IRR but increase the validity of decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance desire for higher IRR against need for diverse perspectives. Design reviewer selection to match goals (consensus vs representation of multiple valid viewpoints).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of structured evaluation instruments / quality scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Structured scoring methods and evaluation sheets (quality scores, structured methods for abstract selection) were cited as interventions that can improve inter-rater agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement standardized rating forms, clear criteria, and appropriate scale points to increase reliability. Report details of these instruments in publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for in-depth studies on causes of reviewer disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Very few studies analyze the substantive reasons behind reviewer disagreement (e.g., content analyses of comment sheets, how reviewers apply standards, leniency/strictness differences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend future research that investigates the processes of judgment (application of criteria, rater severity) to inform interventions aimed at improving IRR and validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of pooled IRR estimates and credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies reporting high IRR are to be considered less credible than those reporting low IRR because high IRR often comes from small-sample studies; meta-analysis that weights by standard error provides more unbiased estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting pooled IRR, prefer estimates from analyses that properly weight by sampling error and account for heterogeneity. Be cautious about taking high IRR at face value when derived from small studies lacking methodological detail.
